# Book I, Proposition 2

*A straight line equal to a given one, placed at a given point*

> To place at a given point (as an extremity) a straight line equal to a given straight line.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/02-idea.svg" alt="The small circle turns the given straight line (blue, upper right) to run on from one red side; the big circle carries it round to the given point, on the other (blue, left). The red sides are equal, so the blue pieces beyond them are equal." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>The small circle turns the given straight line (blue, upper right) to run on from one red side; the big circle carries it round to the given point, on the other (blue, left). The red sides are equal, so the blue pieces beyond them are equal.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/02.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.2, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let A be the given point, and BC the given straight line.

Thus it is required to place at the point A (as an extremity) a straight line equal to the given straight line BC.

From the point A to the point B let the straight line AB be joined; [Post. 1]

and on it let the equilateral triangle DAB be constructed. [I. 1]

Let the straight lines AE, BF be produced in a straight line with DA, DB; [Post. 2]

with centre B and distance BC let the circle CGH be described; [Post. 3]

and again, with centre D and distance DG let the circle GKL be described. [Post. 3]

Then, since the point B is the centre of the circle CGH,

BC is equal to BG.

Again, since the point D is the centre of the circle GKL,

DL is equal to DG.

And in these DA is equal to DB;

therefore the remainder AL is equal to the remainder BG. [C.N. 3]

But BC was also proved equal to BG;

therefore each of the straight lines AL, BC is equal to BG.

And things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another; [C.N. 1]

therefore AL is also equal to BC.

Therefore at the given point A the straight line AL is placed equal to the given straight line BC.

(Being) what it was required to do.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop02.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop02.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- To place at a given point (as an extremity) a straight line equal to a given straight
line. -/
theorem Prop2 (A B C : Point) (hBC : B ≠ C) :
    ∃ L : Point, ‖A L‖ = ‖B C‖ := by
  /- If the given point A is B itself, BC already does the job. Euclid's figure
     has A apart from B, and that is the case his proof treats. -/
  by_cases hAB' : A = B
  · exact ⟨C, by rw [hAB']⟩
  have hAB : A ≠ B := hAB'
  -- Let A be the given point, and BC the given straight line.
  -- Thus it is required to place at the point A (as an extremity) a straight line equal to
  -- the given straight line BC.
  -- From the point A to the point B let the straight line AB be joined; [Post. 1]
  -- and on it let the equilateral triangle DAB be constructed. [I. 1]
  /- Either side of AB will do, so no side is named: the point given for a side
     is A itself, which is on AB. -/
  obtain ⟨D, ⟨hABD, -, hBD_DA⟩, -⟩ := Prop1 A B hAB A
  have hDA_DB : ‖D A‖ = ‖D B‖ := hBD_DA.symm.trans (len_symm B D)
  have hDB : D ≠ B := hABD.ne₂₃.symm
  have hDA : D ≠ A := hABD.ne₁₃.symm
  -- Let the straight lines AE, BF be produced in a straight line with DA, DB; [Post. 2]
  obtain ⟨DF, hD_DF, hB_DF⟩ := Postulate1 D B hDB
  obtain ⟨DE, hD_DE, hA_DE⟩ := Postulate1 D A hDA
  -- with centre B and distance BC let the circle CGH be described; [Post. 3]
  obtain ⟨CGH, hB_CGH, hC_CGH⟩ := Postulate3 B C hBC
  /- Euclid's point G is where DB, produced beyond B, meets the circle CGH
     (System E, Intersections 5): B is the centre, so it lies inside. -/
  obtain ⟨G, hG_CGH, -, hGBD⟩ :=
    line_circle_beyond (centre_inside hB_CGH) hB_DF hD_DF hDB
  have hDBG : Between D B G := between_symm hGBD
  have hDG : D ≠ G := ne_of_between_ends hDBG
  -- and again, with centre D and distance DG let the circle GKL be described. [Post. 3]
  obtain ⟨GKL, hD_GKL, hG_GKL⟩ := Postulate3 D G hDG
  /- And L is where DA, produced beyond A, meets the circle GKL. That needs A
     inside GKL, which holds because DA is equal to DB, and DB is only a part
     of DG. -/
  have hDB_BG : ‖D B‖ + ‖B G‖ = ‖D G‖ := len_add_of_between hDBG
  have hA_GKL : InsideCircle A GKL := by
    apply inside_of_len_lt hD_GKL hG_GKL
    rw [hDA_DB, ← hDB_BG]
    exact CommonNotion5 (len_pos (ne_of_between hGBD).symm)
  obtain ⟨L, hL_GKL, -, hLAD⟩ := line_circle_beyond hA_GKL hA_DE hD_DE hDA
  -- Then, since the point B is the centre of the circle CGH,
  -- BC is equal to BG.
  have hBC_BG : ‖B C‖ = ‖B G‖ := Definition15 hB_CGH hC_CGH hG_CGH
  -- Again, since the point D is the centre of the circle GKL,
  -- DL is equal to DG.
  have hDL_DG : ‖D L‖ = ‖D G‖ := Definition15 hD_GKL hL_GKL hG_GKL
  -- And in these DA is equal to DB;
  have hDA_AL : ‖D A‖ + ‖A L‖ = ‖D L‖ := len_add_of_between (between_symm hLAD)
  -- therefore the remainder AL is equal to the remainder BG. [C.N. 3]
  have hAL_BG : ‖A L‖ = ‖B G‖ := by
    apply CommonNotion3 (c := ‖D A‖) (d := ‖D B‖) _ hDA_DB
    rw [add_comm, hDA_AL, hDL_DG, ← hDB_BG, add_comm]
  -- But BC was also proved equal to BG;
  -- therefore each of the straight lines AL, BC is equal to BG.
  -- And things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another; [C.N. 1]
  -- therefore AL is also equal to BC.
  have hAL_BC : ‖A L‖ = ‖B C‖ := CommonNotion1 hAL_BG hBC_BG
  -- Therefore at the given point A the straight line AL is placed equal to the given straight
  -- line BC.
  exact ⟨L, hAL_BC⟩
  -- (Being) what it was required to do.
```

## Mishnah

**A compass that closes.** Why can we not simply draw a circle about A with radius BC? Proclus calls that a *petitio principii*, a begging of the question (Heath, vol. 1, p. 246): Postulate 3 lets us draw a circle with a given centre through a given point, and nothing more. Augustus De Morgan, quoted by Heath, asks us to "suppose the compasses to close of themselves the moment they cease to touch the paper. These two propositions [I. 2, 3] extend the power of construction to what it would have been if *all* the usual power of the compasses had been assumed" (vol. 1, p. 246). I.2 does its share with an equilateral triangle and two circles.

**One case, or many?** Proclus sorts this proposition into cases by where A lies. Heath answers that "Euclid's method is to give one case only, for choice the most difficult, leaving the reader to supply the rest for himself" (vol. 1, p. 246). Lean cannot be left to supply anything, yet our proof covers every position at once: the rules that find G and L say only that DB and DA, produced, cut their circles, wherever they lie. One case it must set apart: A at B itself, with no straight line AB to build on. There, as Heath says of Proclus' point at an end, "we are given what we are required to find" (vol. 1, p. 245).

**Where does L come from?** Euclid produces DA and DB (Postulate 2) before drawing his circles. Lean needs no Postulate 2 here: G and L come straight from the rule that a straight line through the inside of a circle, produced, meets it (System E, Intersections 5). That rule wants A inside the circle GKL, which holds because DA is equal to DB, and DB is only part of DG: the whole is greater than the part, Common Notion 5, used here without a word from Euclid.

**The modern way.** In vectors, the point A + (C − B) is as far from A as C is from B, but sliding BC over to A, parallel to itself, keeps its length only by I.34, which rests on Postulate 5. Euclid's L needs no parallels: it lies on DA produced, at A + |BC| u, where u is the unit vector from D towards A.
